cards.title: Swipe philosophies, not copy, to build ad frameworks
cards.summary: Extract the reusable psychological framework behind a winning ad instead of rewriting its copy for your niche.
cards.use_when: You are researching acquisition creative for a new product launch and deciding what to model your ad angles and hooks on.
steps: Collect ads or brand assets that are already performing in adjacent or same-category markets as reference data.
For each, don't transcribe the copy. Instead ask: what belief is being installed, what mechanism is claimed, what objection is being pre-empted, and in what order?
Write the extracted pattern as a reusable framework (e.g. 'problem-agitate-unconventional-cause-proof-offer') that drops into any niche.
File these frameworks in a persistent library so each new campaign starts from accumulated patterns, not a blank page.
When you do adapt a single ad closely, treat it as a shortcut that expires; the underlying framework is what keeps working when the creative is fatigued.
Feed your framework library into whatever AI writing tool you use so generated variants inherit the principle, not one competitor's wording.
caveats: The source argues one-to-one swiping works a little but does not build durable skill; that is the presenter's opinion, not a measured rule.
Do not copy a competitor's claims or proof points into your own ads — only the structural pattern.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Remove variables: launch on proven demand
cards.summary: Before adding a new product, ad or offer, eliminate the unknowns you can control — especially unproven product demand.
cards.use_when: You are selecting a product to launch or deciding whether to test an entirely new, never-before-sold SKU.
steps: List the variables that determine whether a launch succeeds: media buying, creative, copy, hook, product, market, platform algorithm, etc. The source claims this list can run to 30-40 items.
Cross off anything you can control or verify before testing — most importantly, whether people already buy this category of product.

Prefer markets where demand is already validated: people searching, competitors selling, reviews and category spend already exist. The source says the strongest marketers he knows hunt for proven markets, not unicorns.
Run experiments that change one variable at a time so a result can be attributed; a totally unproven product stacks an extra unknown on top of every other unknown.
Treat 'success is subtraction' as the presenter's framing: the goal is to reduce the number of things that could explain a failed launch.
caveats: The presenter notes that an unproven unicorn product can occasionally win big — he explicitly allows for the exception but argues it's unnecessary risk for most.
The 30-40 variable estimate is a rhetorical figure, not a measured count.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Optimize ads for clarity, not production polish
cards.summary: The source argues ugly, clear ads often outspend cinematic ones; stop optimizing for aesthetics and optimize for message clarity.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a creative team, editing a video ad, or deciding whether to spend budget on higher production value for your store's paid creative.
steps: Read the ad without visuals: does a stranger understand what you sell, who it's for, why it's different and what to do next within the first seconds?
Identify which elements exist only for aesthetics (cinematic b-roll, trend-sound montage, brand film) and cut or demote them if they delay the promise.
Put the strongest claim, the clearest demonstration and the reason to believe in the earliest frames you can.
When comparing a polished and a plain version, test the plain version against the same audience and offer; judge on conversion and spend, not on how the ad looks to you.
Recognize that the presenter's claim is that the clarity of the copy, not ugliness itself, drives the result — there is no proportional 'uglier = more money' rule.
caveats: This is the source's stated opinion based on his own ads; it is not a universal law and some polished creative does perform.
Clarity-first creative still has to comply with platform creative quality rules and brand standards.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Optimize the three economics: ads, funnel, backend
cards.summary: Break business economics into ad economics, funnel economics and backend economics, each with its own two-sided objective.
cards.use_when: You are setting targets for your store's ad account and funnel, or diagnosing which layer is underperforming.
steps: Ads layer: track ad spend, CPM, CPC and CTR. Objective is the lowest cost of traffic at the highest quality — the source warns that the cheapest traffic (e.g. sub-$1 CPM in some geos) is worthless if those users don't buy.
Funnel layer: track conversion rate and average order value (AOV). Objective is the most conversions at the highest possible AOV per order.
Backend layer: track repeat purchase rate, subscriptions, MRR/ARR. Objective is maximizing customer lifetime value (LTV) — the average total cash a customer produces over their relationship with you.
Example of the distinction: a $100 purchase means AOV $100 and LTV $100; if that customer buys again in a few months, LTV becomes $200 while AOV stays $100.
Work the three together: cheap qualified traffic, high conversions at high AOV, then lift LTV via subscription, replenishment or ascension offers.
Note the presenter's disagreement with the camp that says pick either high AOV or an LTV/repeat play — he asserts you can run both.
caveats: The high-AOV-plus-strong-LTV position is the presenter's opinion and he acknowledges it is debatable.
Platform metric names and definitions change; verify current reporting definitions before building dashboards on them.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Use AOV and LTV as levers on your ad bids
cards.summary: A higher-value customer lets you outbid competitors for the same auction because acquiring a customer is the hard part.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in AOV-raising bundles, upsells or post-purchase offers rather than only optimizing ad creative.
steps: Compute your customer acquisition cost (CAC) and your average revenue per customer from one purchase (AOV).
Compute total revenue per acquired customer over time (LTV) for your store — repeat orders, subscriptions, ascension offers.

If two sellers pay the same $50 CAC but one's customer is worth $80 and yours is worth $100, the source argues you can now spend up to roughly $70 to acquire a customer while the competitor can only sustain $50.
Treat 'the business that can afford to spend the most to acquire a customer wins' as a quoted Dan Kennedy line cited by the presenter, not a proof about your auction.
Raise AOV through bundles, cross-sells, minimum-order offers or plan tiers, and raise LTV through subscription/replenishment or a clear next step after purchase.
Reinvest the extra margin into your bidding headroom to pursue growth rather than only margin.
caveats: The $50/$80/$100 example is illustrative; margins, refunds and fees mean the real extra spendable amount is smaller than the gross difference.
Platform auction mechanics are not purely bid-driven, so extra headroom does not guarantee you win a given impression.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Target a 3:1 LTV-to-CAC ratio as a baseline
cards.summary: LTV:CAC is the source's baseline business health metric, with different targets depending on business model.
cards.use_when: Sanity-checking whether your store's acquisition cost is sustainable before scaling ad spend or raising budgets.
steps: Compute LTV as the average total cash collected from a customer over their lifetime with your brand.
Compute CAC as the blended cost to acquire a customer, including ad spend and media costs.
Divide LTV by CAC to get the ratio; the source suggests 3:1 as a bare minimum for most models.
If the ratio is comfortable, put additional cash back into acquisition to scale; the source notes that scaling often makes CAC worse and requires more creative, so headroom matters.
Recompute the ratio for your model — the source says high-ticket models run very different KPIs from ecom.
caveats: The 3:1 baseline and the 7-10:1 high-ticket range are the source's heuristics, not an industry calculation you should treat as a hard threshold.
LTV assumptions based on projected repeat rates can flatter the ratio; use actual cohort data where possible.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Build retention into the backend from day one
cards.summary: The source argues mastery of LTV is the most common driver in sustainably scaled businesses, achieved through subscription, replenishment or ascension.
cards.use_when: Designing whether your store should push subscriptions or replenishment offers versus one-off purchases.
steps: Map your current repeat purchase rate and the intervals at which customers naturally reorder.

For consumable categories, offer a subscription or auto-replenish option that matches a realistic reorder cadence (the source cites 30-, 60- or 90-day cycles) and make it available at checkout or post-purchase.
For non-consumable or service-like offers, design a next step to move customers up rather than relying on repeated identical purchases.
Track repeat purchase rate and customer LTV as their own KPIs, not as a byproduct of ad reporting.
Recognize that when repeat purchase is zero, LTV equals AOV — the source treats that as a backend constraint to fix.
Accept that CAC is unlikely to fall as you scale; the source argues you'll need to keep adding new creative, so retention is the more durable lever.
caveats: Subscription and replenishment mechanics vary by payment platform and region — verify the current implementation.
Forcing all buyers into subscription can raise friction or cancellations; the source presents it as the norm in consumable categories, not a universal rule.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Treat platform-attributed data as approximate
cards.summary: Post-tracking-policy ad-platform reporting can over- or under-attribute by double digits, so verify with an independent source.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to kill or scale an ad based solely on metrics shown inside the ad platform.
steps: Assume in-platform conversion counts can be off in either direction — the source estimates anywhere from 5-10% on the low end up to 30-50% on the high end.
Use a third-party attribution or analytics tool alongside platform data to establish your own reconciled conversion count.
Reconcile the differences before you make budget decisions; the source warns you can otherwise optimize toward ads that are actually losing money.
Set a policy for which number you trust for reporting, and apply it consistently so scaling decisions aren't based on noise.
Re-check attribution periodically — the source notes platform and OS updates have changed definitions of counts like landing page views and content views.
caveats: The 5-10%/30-50% error ranges are the presenter's estimates, not a measured benchmark, and specific values will drift with platform and privacy-policy changes.
Third-party attribution tools also have limitations; no single source should be treated as exact.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Find the constraint, not the symptom
cards.summary: A bad conversion rate or high checkout drop-off is an indicator of a constraint, not the constraint itself — the source's 'hose' model.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a funnel step underperforms before spending on redesign or new creative.
steps: Picture the business as a hose; kinks are constraints, and water is traffic and orders.
Track drop-off and KPIs for every funnel step: ad metrics (CPC, CPM, CTR), then landing page view-to-add-to-cart, add-to-cart-to-checkout, and checkout-to-purchase.
Example the source gives: healthy CPM, CPC and CTR with a weak conversion rate is not a constraint — it's a signal that the funnel is the bottleneck, so look deeper.
Example of a real root cause: a very high checkout-page drop-off traced to the store's payment processor not being set up at all.
Focus all effort on the identified constraint until flow improves, then re-measure, since constraint moves as you scale.
caveats: The source warns you will not see every constraint in your own business; partners or outside reviewers can surface what you miss.
A single funnel-step metric can have multiple causes; the point is to instrument each step so you can trace where the loss occurs.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Try to break your funnel before you launch
cards.summary: The source recommends aggressively trying to break your own funnel rather than only quality-checking it — customers will find the gaps if you don't.
cards.use_when: Running pre-launch QA on a new product page, checkout flow, offer or landing page.
steps: Walk the complete purchase path yourself as a first-time visitor: ad or entry point, landing page, product selection, cart, checkout, payment, confirmation.
Test payments deliberately — the source's example was a funnel with high checkout abandonment because the payment processor was never actually set up.
Test failure paths and edge cases: sold-out variants, expired coupons, discount stacking, mobile keyboards, address fields, and post-purchase emails.
Attempt to break the experience on purpose (back button, refresh mid-checkout, interrupted payment) rather than only confirming the happy path works.
Fix what you find before spending on traffic; the source describes launching untested funnels as common and avoidable.
caveats: This is a pre-launch QA discipline, not permission to test real customer funds or commit fraud.
Test environments may behave differently from live payment systems — verify with a real low-value transaction when acceptable.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Use entropy thinking to plan scaling headroom
cards.summary: The source argues systems drift toward disorder as you scale, and only deliberate added energy — time, people or systems — keeps things working.
cards.use_when: Planning how to keep operations — fulfillment, creative pipeline and ad management — intact while increasing order volume.
steps: Assume things you built will degrade, including a winning creative, offer or copy that has been performing; the source treats decay as a fundamental law rather than a failure.
Identify where the bottleneck will appear first as volume grows — creative production, order processing, support or inventory.
Inject one of three forms of 'energy' the source names: your own hours (limited), hires/human capital, or systems and AI tools.

For an ecommerce operation, examples of injecting energy could mean another creative editor, a product data/feed system or an AI-assisted merchandising workflow — but choose based on your actual bottleneck.
Keep external review in place so problems are caught before they compound, since the source argues you cannot see all issues in your own business alone.
Reassess as you scale, because the source claims everything gets harder, including rising CAC, not easier.
caveats: Entropy is used as a metaphor from physics; it is not a predictive model for business outcomes.
Adding people or tools without fixing the actual constraint adds cost without improving throughput.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Treat 'intuition' as accumulated test data, not a launch signal
cards.summary: The source argues gut feel about a product or ad represents pattern experience, and that beginners without test history are mostly rationalizing a cognitive bias.
cards.use_when: You feel certain a product or creative will work and are about to launch it without validated demand.
steps: Ask how many tests in this category you have personally observed — the source frames the claimed 10,000 to 20,000 hours of accumulated data as the basis for useful pattern sense.
If you don't have that history, treat your feeling as a hypothesis to test rather than a reason to commit budget.
Even with experience, the source states he is still wrong frequently — build in the expectation that any given test may fail.
Convert the hypothesis into a structured test with defined variables and success criteria instead of scaling on conviction.
For product selection specifically, replace 'I can feel it' with evidence that people already buy the category.
caveats: This is the presenter's strongly held opinion, delivered bluntly — treat it as a caution against unsupported confidence rather than a rule that experience means nothing.
Experience genuinely does improve judgment in some settings; the source's point is about the unverifiable confidence of beginners.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Simulate customer conversations with AI avatars
cards.summary: When you lack customer research access, the source suggests building AI personas from your research docs to rehearse and mine customer language.
cards.use_when: You need customer insight for copy or positioning but have no customers, can't run interviews, or need more angles.
steps: Write down your research: audience beliefs, objections, prior purchases and buying triggers, ideally from real data if you have it.
Build a small bot or prompt that instructs an AI to act as a specific customer who holds those beliefs — the source suggests one persona per buying angle.
Add your research material as the knowledge source so the persona draws on your findings rather than generic assumptions.
Conduct the conversation hands-free (the source describes walking while talking with earbuds) and ask what made them buy, what they feared and what they compared.
Capture verbatim language and objections to reuse in ads, PDP copy and offer framing.
Repeat across personas to compare angles before committing spend.
caveats: AI personas reflect the inputs you give them; they are not evidence of real customer behavior and should not replace actual customer data when it is available.
Do not confuse simulated insight with validated market research.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx

cards.title: Keep pushing AI capability past the 'chatbot' stage
cards.summary: The source frames AI as a multiplier across every metric and urges operators to stay current as capability evolves.
cards.use_when: Deciding how deeply to adopt AI across your store's marketing, operations or support rather than only using one chat tool.
steps: Treat LLM chat as the entry level: useful for copy, research synthesis and analysis.
Move to workflows where tools are chained to complete repeatable tasks with less manual input.
Then to individual agents that can autonomously complete a task, and — as capability permits — coordinated multi-agent systems for a single goal.
Apply AI against specific metrics in your economics, rather than only as a creative generator: research, copy variants, image/creative production, customer support, analytics reconciliation.
Build your own urgency about staying current, since the source argues the adoption window narrows as capability becomes mainstream.
Evaluate any new tool against a specific task in your store rather than adopting it for novelty.
caveats: The five-stage ladder (LLMs → workflows → agents → agentic → AGI) is the presenter's framing, not an established taxonomy, and stage labels shift as tools change.
Verify current capabilities and interfaces of any AI tool before designing processes around specific features.
cards.source_name: 8 years of marketing advice in 70 minutes.docx
